Pungi源自印度次大陆，屬印度教民間音樂簧管樂器，主要見於信德、拉賈斯坦、塔爾: The pungi comes from the Indian subcontinent and is a reed pipe of Hindu folk music, found mainly in Sindh, Rajasthan, the Thar Desert, the Terai and Nepal, and played mostly by snake charmers and Jogis. It has an important place in Indian folk culture: in North India it is called been, tumbi or bansi, and in South India magudi, mahudi, pungi or pambaattikulhal. In 1991 India banned snake charming under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, which restricted its use in street performance.

The source states that the body is a dried, hollow gourd or a hard coconut shell, that the two pipes are bamboo, and that the reeds, called jivala, are single reeds that vibrate freely; the material of the other reeds, the way the parts are joined and the details of the fingerholes are not stated. The region is the South Asian subcontinent.

A beginner should concentrate on circular breathing to keep the sound going, while controlling the drone pipe and the melody pipe so that both parts sound at once. The source gives no details of holding position or teaching material, so the description can only follow the way the instrument sounds and is played; it is usually a solo instrument and is hard to combine with others.

Its range lies in the middle and high register, the tone is sharp and penetrating, and outdoors it carries a long way. The instrument resonates through the wind chamber, which gives the tone a faint flutter and produces a hypnotic sound. The pungi lies between the recorder and the bagpipe, more penetrating than the recorder and softer than the bagpipe. Because it is played with circular breathing the sound never stops, forming a continuous stream. The double pipe gives the tone depth and a harmonic effect, and the whole has a warm, faintly uncanny, mysterious character that suits the particular atmosphere of a religious rite or a street performance.

The pungi is an aerophone from the Indian subcontinent, Hornbostel-Sachs number 422.22. It uses a dried gourd or a coconut shell as a wind chamber, joined to two bamboo pipes, each with a reed; the air divides into the two pipes, one sounding a drone, the other playing the melody. The player keeps the sound going with circular breathing, the melody pipe has seven holes, the range is one octave, and it is usually a solo instrument. It is common in Indian folk music, and in the past cobra charmers played it in the street, or in Sindh, Rajasthan, the Thar Desert, the Terai and Nepal for snake dances.
